faq: Is my file uploaded to a server?
No. GeoUnpack runs the open-source GDAL and 7-Zip libraries inside your browser using WebAssembly. Your file never leaves your computer.
Which files can I open?

ArcGIS layer packages (.lpk, .lpkx), map packages (.mpk, .mpkx) and file geodatabases (.gdb folders compressed as .zip). Vector layers and attribute tables are supported. Raster, tile and scene packages are not supported yet.
Do I need ArcGIS or QGIS?
No. You only need a modern browser such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari on a computer.
Is there a size limit?
Files up to 150 MB are supported for now, because everything runs in your browser's memory.
subtitle: Open LPK, MPK and GDB files without ArcGIS. Preview the layers and convert them to Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KML or CSV.

p: Layer packages (`.lpk`, `.lpkx`) and map packages (`.mpk`, `.mpkx`) are 7-Zip archives made by ArcMap or ArcGIS Pro. Inside is a layer or map definition plus a copy of the data, almost always a file geodatabase (`.gdb`) and sometimes shapefiles. A file geodatabase is a folder of binary tables that ArcGIS uses as its native storage.

The data itself is not locked to ArcGIS. The open-source GDAL library reads file geodatabases directly, and GeoUnpack runs GDAL inside your browser, so you get the same result as the command-line route without installing anything.

body.h2: What you get, and what you don't
p: GeoUnpack extracts the data, not the map design.
list: Kept: geometry, all attribute fields, the coordinate system, standalone tables.
Not kept: symbology, labels, layouts, definition queries and joins. Those live in the layer or map definition, which only ArcGIS can render.
Not read yet: raster, tile and scene data, and packages that only reference data on a server instead of containing it.

p: GeoPackage is the safest choice for QGIS and most modern GIS software: one file, long field names, no size cap. Choose Shapefile when the receiving software only accepts it, GeoJSON for web maps and code, KML for Google Earth, and CSV when you only need the attribute table in a spreadsheet.

title: LPK to Shapefile Converter: ArcGIS Layer Package to SHP Online | GeoUnpack
description: Convert .lpk and .lpkx layer packages to Shapefile (.shp) online without ArcGIS. Free, runs in your browser, files are never uploaded.
lead: An .lpk file is a compressed package that holds a layer's data (usually a file geodatabase) and its styling. GeoUnpack unpacks it and exports the data as a zipped Shapefile you can open in QGIS, AutoCAD Map 3D, Global Mapper or any GIS.
steps: Drop the .lpk or .lpkx file into the box.
Select the layer (Preview shows it on a map).
Keep 'SHP (Shapefile)' selected and click Convert & download.
faq: Can I just rename the .lpk to .zip?
Often yes. An .lpk is a 7-Zip archive. You can extract it with 7-Zip and load the .gdb folder in QGIS. GeoUnpack does the same in one step, and also converts the data if you don't have QGIS.
Will the symbology be kept?
No. Shapefiles store geometry and attributes only. Colors, labels and symbols from the .lyr/.lyrx file are not converted.
Why are some field names shortened?
The Shapefile format limits field names to 10 characters and can truncate very large numbers. If exact values matter, export to GeoPackage or GeoJSON instead.
Is this the same as ArcGIS 'Extract Package'?
It extracts the same data. The difference is that you don't need ArcGIS, and the result is converted to Shapefile (or another format) directly.
subtitle: Convert ArcGIS layer packages (.lpk, .lpkx) to Shapefile. No ArcGIS needed.

p: An `.lpk` is a 7-Zip archive. Unpacked, it holds a `.lyr` file (the symbology), an `esriinfo` folder (metadata and a thumbnail) and one or more version folders such as `v10` or `v108`, each with a file geodatabase or shapefiles containing the actual features. When a package holds the same data for several ArcGIS versions, GeoUnpack reads only the newest copy so layers are not listed twice.

body.h2: What changes when you convert to Shapefile
p: Shapefile is an old format with hard limits. GeoUnpack applies the usual workarounds and tells you about them:
list: Field names are cut to 10 characters. `POPULATION_2020` becomes `POPULATION` and a second similar field becomes `POPULATI_1`.
Date-and-time fields keep only the date.
Text longer than 254 characters is truncated, and very large whole numbers can lose digits.
Z values are dropped (`-dim XY`), because mixed 2D/3D geometry makes the export fail.
The coordinate system is kept as is and written to the `.prj` file; text is stored as UTF-8 with a `.cpg` file.

p: If the person or program receiving the data accepts GeoPackage, use it: none of the limits above apply. Pick Shapefile for older software, for upload forms that ask for a zipped shapefile, and for AutoCAD Map 3D or Civil 3D workflows.

title: LPK to KML Converter: Open ArcGIS Layer Packages in Google Earth | GeoUnpack
description: Turn an ArcGIS .lpk or .lpkx layer package into a KML file you can open in Google Earth. Free online, no ArcGIS, no upload.
lead: Got an .lpk but only have Google Earth? GeoUnpack extracts the layer, reprojects it to WGS84 and writes a KML file Google Earth can open.
steps: Drop the .lpk or .lpkx file into the box.
Select the layer you want.
Choose 'KML (Google Earth)' and click Convert & download, then open the file in Google Earth.
faq: Will it line up correctly in Google Earth?
Yes. KML must use WGS84 longitude/latitude, so GeoUnpack reprojects the data automatically from the package's coordinate system.
Does KML keep the attributes?
Yes, attributes are stored as extended data and show in the feature balloon in Google Earth.
subtitle: Convert ArcGIS layer packages to KML and open them in Google Earth.

p: KML only supports latitude and longitude on the WGS84 datum, while layer packages are usually in a projected system such as a UTM zone or State Plane. GeoUnpack reads the layer's coordinate system from the geodatabase and reprojects every vertex to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) before writing the KML, which is why the result lands in the right place in Google Earth.

body.h2: What to expect in Google Earth
list: Every attribute is written into the feature's pop-up balloon.
Colours, line widths and labels from ArcGIS are not carried over; Google Earth applies its default style, which you can change per folder.
Google Earth Pro on a computer handles tens of thousands of features. Google My Maps is much stricter: about 2,000 features per layer and a 5 MB file limit, so export smaller layers for it.
KML is verbose. Expect the file to be several times larger than the same data as a Shapefile.

title: LPK to GeoJSON Converter Online: Free, No Upload | GeoUnpack
description: Convert ArcGIS .lpk and .lpkx layer packages to GeoJSON for web maps (Leaflet, Mapbox, deck.gl). Free and private: runs in your browser.
lead: GeoJSON is the easiest format for web maps and scripts. GeoUnpack converts the layer inside your .lpk to GeoJSON in WGS84 with six-decimal precision.
steps: Drop the .lpk or .lpkx file into the box.
Select one or more layers.
Choose 'GeoJSON' and click Convert & download.
faq: What coordinate system does the GeoJSON use?
WGS84 (EPSG:4326), as required by the GeoJSON specification.
My GeoJSON is very large. Why?
GeoJSON is plain text and detailed polygons produce big files. For large layers, GeoPackage is more compact.
subtitle: Convert ArcGIS layer packages to GeoJSON (WGS84) for web maps and scripts.

p: The output is one `FeatureCollection` per layer, following RFC 7946: coordinates are longitude, latitude in WGS84, rounded to six decimals (about 10 cm on the ground). Attribute fields become `properties` with their full names, since GeoJSON has no 10-character limit. Single and multi-part geometries are written as multi-part (`MultiPolygon`, `MultiLineString`) so every feature in a layer has the same type, which keeps Leaflet, Mapbox GL and geopandas code simple.

body.h2: When GeoJSON is the wrong choice
p: GeoJSON is plain text, so a layer with detailed boundaries can reach hundreds of megabytes and become slow to load in a web map. For large layers export GeoPackage instead, or simplify the geometry afterwards with a tool such as mapshaper. If you need the original projected coordinates rather than WGS84, GeoPackage and Shapefile keep them.

title: How to Open an LPK File Without ArcGIS: 3 Free Ways | GeoUnpack
h1: Open an LPK File Without ArcGIS
description: No ArcGIS licence? Open an .lpk layer package for free: convert it online in your browser, unpack it with 7-Zip and use QGIS, or run GDAL. Works on Windows and Mac.
lead: You don't need an ArcGIS licence to get the data out of an .lpk. Use the tool below, or follow one of the free manual methods further down.
steps: Easiest: drop the .lpk below and export to Shapefile, GeoPackage or KML.
With QGIS: extract the .lpk with 7-Zip, then drag the .gdb folder from the 'v10'/'v108' subfolder into QGIS.
With GDAL: extract it, then run ogr2ogr -f GPKG out.gpkg path/to/data.gdb.
faq: Which method should I use?
If you already have QGIS, method 2 is free and keeps everything local. If you don't want to install anything, use the online tool. It also runs locally in your browser.
Can I edit the data?
Once exported to Shapefile or GeoPackage you can edit it in any GIS. The original .lpk is not changed.
ArcMap says “Invalid package. Error reading package contents.” Will this still work?

Often, yes. That message comes from the ArcGIS package handler, for example when the package was made in a newer ArcGIS version. GeoUnpack reads the archive without it. It cannot help if the download is incomplete or the package contains no vector data.
subtitle: Use the converter below, or follow one of the free manual methods further down.

body.h2: Method 1: convert it in the browser
p: Drop the file into the tool at the top of this page. It lists the layers, previews them and exports Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KML or CSV. Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded. This is the quickest route if you only need the data once.

body.h2: Method 2: unpack it with 7-Zip and open it in QGIS
p: An `.lpk` is a 7-Zip archive. Install the free 7-Zip (Windows) or Keka (Mac), right-click the file and extract it. Renaming it to `.zip` does not help: Windows reports “The Compressed (zipped) Folder … is invalid”, because the built-in zip tools expect zip compression; recent Windows 11 versions can open it if you rename it to `.7z`. Inside, open the version folder with the highest number (for example `v108`) and find the folder ending in `.gdb`. In QGIS, drag that folder onto the map window, or use Layer › Add Layer › Add Vector Layer with source type Directory.

body.h2: Method 3: GDAL on the command line
p: After extracting as in method 2, GDAL converts the geodatabase in one line: `ogr2ogr -f GPKG output.gpkg path/to/data.gdb`. Use `ogrinfo path/to/data.gdb` first to list the layers. This is the best option for many files or for automation.

body.h2: What about ArcGIS Online or ArcGIS Earth?
p: You can upload a layer package to ArcGIS Online as an item, but that only stores it so others can download it into ArcGIS desktop software; it is not drawn on a web map. In practice the three methods above are the ones that work without a licence.

title: Open an LPK File in QGIS: 2 Free Ways (Step by Step) | GeoUnpack
h1: Open an LPK File in QGIS
description: QGIS can't open .lpk files directly. Convert the layer package to GeoPackage in your browser in one step, or unpack it with 7-Zip and load the .gdb. Both methods explained.
lead: QGIS doesn't recognise .lpk or .mpk files, but the data inside is a normal file geodatabase. Convert it to GeoPackage with the tool above and drag the result into QGIS, or unpack it by hand with the steps below.
steps: Fastest: drop the .lpk above, choose GPKG and click Convert & download. Drag the .gpkg into QGIS.
By hand: open the .lpk with 7-Zip (it is a 7-Zip archive; renaming it to .7z also works) and extract it.
In the extracted folder, open the 'v10', 'v106' or 'v108' subfolder and find the folder ending in .gdb.
In QGIS, drag that .gdb folder onto the map, or use Layer > Add Layer > Add Vector Layer > Directory > OpenFileGDB.
faq: Why can't QGIS open the .lpk directly?
An .lpk is a 7-Zip archive that bundles a file geodatabase with ArcGIS layer styling. QGIS reads the geodatabase but not the package wrapper, so it has to be extracted or converted first.
Will the styling come across?
No. Colours and labels are stored in an ArcGIS-only format. You get the geometry and attributes; restyle the layer in QGIS.
GeoPackage or Shapefile for QGIS?
GeoPackage. It keeps long field names, multiple layers in one file and has no 2 GB limit. Use Shapefile only if someone else needs it.
subtitle: QGIS can't read .lpk packages directly. Convert or unpack first: both ways below.

body.h2: The manual way, step by step
list: Install 7-Zip (Windows) or Keka (Mac). Right-click the `.lpk` or `.mpk` and extract it. Renaming to `.zip` does not work: Windows answers “The Compressed (zipped) Folder … is invalid”, because the package is a 7-Zip archive.
Open the extracted folder. You will see `esriinfo`, a `.lyr` or `.mxd` file, and version folders such as `v10` and `v108`. Go into the highest version.
Find the folder whose name ends in `.gdb`. That is the file geodatabase.
In QGIS choose Layer › Add Layer › Add Vector Layer, set Source type to Directory, pick OpenFileGDB, browse to the `.gdb` folder and click Add. Or simply drag the `.gdb` folder onto the QGIS window.
Tick the layers you want in the dialog that appears.

“Invalid Data Source: … is not a valid or recognized data source”: you selected a file inside the `.gdb` folder instead of the folder itself, or dragged in the `.lpk` itself. QGIS needs the extracted `.gdb` folder.
Every layer appears twice: you loaded the geodatabases from two version folders. Use only the newest.
Layers load but are empty or missing: the package references data that was not included, or the layer is a raster.
The `.lyr` file does nothing in QGIS: it is Esri's symbology format. You will need to style the layer again.

title: Error Reading Package Contents (LPK/MPK): What to Try | GeoUnpack
description: ArcMap says “Invalid package. Error reading package contents.” when opening an .lpk or .mpk? See the usual causes, and get the data out in your browser without ArcGIS.
lead: This message comes from the ArcGIS package handler, not from the data itself. Drop the package below: GeoUnpack opens it without the ArcGIS file handler and lists the layers inside.
subtitle: ArcGIS won’t open the package? Check the causes below, or extract the layers here.
steps: Drop the .lpk, .mpk, .lpkx or .mpkx that ArcGIS refused into the box below.
Wait for the layer list. If layers appear, the package itself is fine and the problem was on the ArcGIS side.
Choose GeoPackage, Shapefile or another format and click Convert & download.
If GeoUnpack can’t open it either, the file is probably incomplete: download it again or ask the sender for a new copy.
faq: Does “Error reading package contents” mean the file is broken?
Not necessarily. Esri lists version differences, a blocked or misconfigured file handler and folder permissions as causes. If GeoUnpack lists the layers, the package itself is readable.
Can I get the symbology or the map layout back?
No. GeoUnpack exports geometry and attributes only. Styling, labels and the .mxd or .mapx layout need ArcGIS.
Is the package uploaded anywhere?
No. It is unpacked and converted inside your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

p: In ArcMap (ArcGIS Desktop) the exact text is usually `Invalid package` followed by `Error reading package contents.` It appears when the ArcGIS package handler (`ArcGISFileHandler.exe`) cannot unpack a layer or map package. Esri’s support articles name several causes: the package was made in a newer ArcGIS version, or one with service packs the recipient lacks; the unpacking folder is not writable or the Documents folder is redirected; or, in ArcMap 10.8.2, Windows Security’s Controlled folder access blocks the handler. Note also that ArcMap cannot open the newer .lpkx and .mpkx packages from ArcGIS Pro at all.

body.h2: Fixes to try in ArcGIS first
list: Save the package to a local drive, then right-click it in ArcCatalog and choose Unpack, or use the Extract Package tool.
Ask which ArcGIS version made the package. Opening it in the same or a newer version is the reliable route.
If Windows Security reports “Controlled folder access blocked ArcGISFileHandler.exe”, allow that app (administrator rights needed).
Run `ArcGISFileHandler.exe` and set a package location you can write to.

body.h2: What GeoUnpack can and cannot fix
p: GeoUnpack does not use the ArcGIS handler. It opens the package as a 7-Zip archive and reads the file geodatabase or shapefiles inside with GDAL, so version mismatches, blocked handlers and folder settings don’t matter. It cannot help when the download is truncated or corrupted, when the package holds only rasters or tiles, or when the package only references data on a server or enterprise geodatabase instead of including it: in that case the data simply isn’t in the file.

title: QGIS: GDB “Is Not a Valid or Recognized Data Source” Fix | GeoUnpack
h1: QGIS: “Is Not a Valid or Recognized Data Source”
description: QGIS says a .gdb or .lpk “is not a valid or recognized data source”? Learn the common causes, the right way to add a file geodatabase, and a browser converter to GeoPackage.
lead: QGIS shows this message when no driver can read what you gave it. Often the fix is just choosing the .gdb folder the right way; if not, convert the data to GeoPackage below and drag that into QGIS.
subtitle: QGIS won’t load the geodatabase or package? Check the causes, or convert it to GeoPackage here.
steps: Zip the whole .gdb folder (right-click › Compress or Send to › Compressed folder). For an .lpk or .mpk, use the file as it is.
Drop the .zip or the package into the box below and wait for the layer list.
Keep GeoPackage selected and click Convert & download.
Drag the .gpkg file into QGIS. All layers and long field names are kept.
faq: Why does QGIS show this for an .lpk or .mpk file?
QGIS has no driver for Esri package files, so it treats them as unknown. Extract the .gdb from the package first, or convert the package to GeoPackage with the tool above.
Will converting fix a geodatabase that holds rasters?
No. GeoUnpack exports vector layers and tables only. For raster datasets inside a .gdb, use a QGIS build with GDAL 3.7 or newer, or ArcGIS.
Do I lose anything by converting to GeoPackage?
Geometry, attributes and the coordinate system are kept. Symbology, labels and other ArcGIS layer settings are not, so you restyle the layers in QGIS.

p: In the QGIS message bar or log it reads `Invalid Data Source: /path/to/name.gdb is not a valid or recognized data source.` It is QGIS’s general message for “no driver could open this”, so the cause is not always the geodatabase itself.

list: You picked a file inside the `.gdb` folder (such as a `.gdbtable`), or used the File source type. Use Layer › Add Layer › Add Vector Layer, set Source type to Directory, choose OpenFileGDB and select the `.gdb` folder itself.
You dragged in an `.lpk`, `.mpk` or a `.zip` that wraps the folder in another folder. QGIS needs the extracted `.gdb`.
The geodatabase holds raster datasets. GDAL, which QGIS uses, reads file geodatabase rasters only from version 3.7; check Help › About for your GDAL version.
On macOS, a QGIS bug report (#18178) describes this error for a `.gdb` on an external exFAT drive that opened after copying it to another drive.
The folder is incomplete, for example copied without all its files, or still being synced.

body.h2: What GeoUnpack can and cannot fix
p: If the problem is the package wrapper or the way the folder was added, GeoUnpack gets you a clean GeoPackage that QGIS always opens. It runs its own copy of GDAL in your browser, so an older GDAL in your QGIS install doesn’t matter for vector layers. It cannot recover a damaged or incomplete geodatabase, and it does not export rasters.

title: “Compressed (Zipped) Folder Is Invalid” for LPK or MPK Files | GeoUnpack
h1: “The Compressed (Zipped) Folder Is Invalid” for .lpk and .mpk
description: Renamed an .lpk or .mpk to .zip and Windows says the compressed (zipped) folder is invalid? These packages are 7-Zip archives. Open them with 7-Zip or convert them in your browser.
lead: Esri layer and map packages are usually 7-Zip archives, not zip files, so renaming them to .zip makes Windows refuse them. Drop the original file below to get the layers out without renaming anything.
subtitle: Windows won’t open the renamed package? Drop the original file here instead.
steps: Rename the file back to its original extension (.lpk, .lpkx, .mpk or .mpkx). GeoUnpack also accepts it as .zip or .7z, but the original name is safest.
Drop it into the box below. GeoUnpack unpacks the 7-Zip archive in your browser.
Pick the layers and an output format, then click Convert & download.
faq: Is my package damaged?
Usually not. Windows’ built-in zip tool cannot read 7-Zip archives and reports them as invalid. If 7-Zip or GeoUnpack can open the file, it is fine.
Can I rename it to .7z instead?
Recent Windows 11 versions can open .7z archives in File Explorer, and 7-Zip (Windows) or Keka (Mac) open the file without any renaming.
What will I find inside?
A file geodatabase (.gdb folder) or shapefiles inside version folders such as v10 or v108, plus Esri layer or map files that only ArcGIS reads.

p: Windows File Explorer shows `Windows cannot open the folder.` followed by `The Compressed (zipped) Folder “C:\…\name.zip” is invalid.` You get it when you rename a `.lpk`, `.lpkx`, `.mpk` or `.mpkx` to `.zip` and double-click it.

A zip file starts with the bytes `PK`; the layer and map packages we have tested start with `7z`, the signature of a 7-Zip archive. A post on the Esri Community Python blog reached the same conclusion for an ArcGIS Pro `.lpkx`, and a commenter notes that Esri uses zip for some other package types. Explorer’s “Compressed (zipped) Folder” feature only understands zip, so it calls the file invalid even though nothing is wrong with it. The same message can also appear for a real zip whose paths are too long for Windows; 7-Zip handles that case too.

body.h2: What GeoUnpack can and cannot fix
p: GeoUnpack reads the 7-Zip archive directly, finds the file geodatabase or shapefiles and exports them. It cannot rebuild a file that was cut off during download, and it won’t find vector layers in packages that contain only rasters or tiles, or that only reference data stored on a server.

What's the difference between .lpk and .lpkx?
.lpk comes from ArcMap, .lpkx from ArcGIS Pro. Both are 7-Zip archives containing the layer data.
subtitle: Convert ArcGIS Pro layer packages (.lpkx) to Shapefile, GeoPackage or GeoJSON.

p: ArcGIS Pro writes `.lpkx`; ArcMap wrote `.lpk`. Both are 7-Zip archives, but an `.lpkx` stores the layer definition as a `.lyrx` file (JSON) and puts the data in folders named after the Pro version, such as `p20` or `p30`, alongside `commondata`. The data is still a file geodatabase, so it converts the same way.

list: ArcGIS Pro layer names and field names are often long. Shapefile cuts field names to 10 characters; choose GeoPackage if you want them intact.
3D layers lose their Z values in Shapefile export. GeoPackage and GeoJSON keep them.
An `.lpkx` made from a raster, mosaic, scene or tile layer has no vector data to export, and GeoUnpack will tell you so.
Packages created with “reference all data” contain only pointers to a network drive or enterprise database; ask the author to share it with the data included.

body.h2: What is inside a map package
p: A map package is a 7-Zip archive holding the map document (`.mxd` for ArcMap `.mpk`, `.mapx` for ArcGIS Pro `.mpkx`) and a copy of the data for every layer in the map. The data usually sits in one or more file geodatabases, sometimes next to loose shapefiles, and is often duplicated for different ArcGIS versions. GeoUnpack scans all of it, keeps the newest copy, and shows one row per layer or table, labelled with the geodatabase it comes from when there are several.

body.h2: What you can and cannot see

You can see standalone and related tables, including attachment tables (names ending in `__ATTACH`).
You cannot see the map layout, layer order, symbology or labels; those are in the map document, which only ArcGIS opens.
Basemaps are not in the package at all. They are online services the map pointed to.

subtitle: Export every layer in an ArcGIS map package to Shapefile in one download.

p: Tick as many layers as you need and click Convert. GeoUnpack writes one Shapefile per layer and puts them in a single `.zip`, with one folder per layer holding its `.shp`, `.shx`, `.dbf`, `.prj` and `.cpg` files. Tables without geometry cannot be Shapefiles, so they are added to the same download as CSV.

body.h2: Why Shapefile needs one file per layer
p: A Shapefile stores a single layer with a single geometry type, which is why a map package with ten layers becomes ten Shapefiles. Relationships between layers and tables are not preserved, though the key fields they were built on are still in the attribute tables, so you can re-create joins in QGIS. If the receiving software accepts it, export GeoPackage instead: you still get one file per layer, but each is a single `.gpkg` rather than five sidecar files, with none of the limits below.
Field names are shortened to 10 characters, date-times keep only the date, and text over 254 characters is cut. The message shown after export reminds you of these.

title: GDB to Shapefile Converter: File Geodatabase to SHP Online | GeoUnpack
description: Convert Esri file geodatabase feature classes to Shapefile online. Zip your .gdb folder, drop it in, export. No ArcGIS, no upload.

Drop the .zip into the box.

faq: Why do I need to zip the .gdb folder?
Browsers can only receive single files. Zipping the folder keeps all of its internal files together.
Are feature datasets supported?
Yes, feature classes inside feature datasets are listed like any other layer.
subtitle: Convert file geodatabase feature classes to Shapefile. Zip the .gdb folder first.

body.h2: How to zip a file geodatabase correctly
p: A file geodatabase looks like a folder named `something.gdb` full of files such as `a00000001.gdbtable`. Zip the folder itself, not the files inside it: on Windows right-click the `.gdb` folder and choose Send to › Compressed (zipped) folder; on a Mac right-click and choose Compress. A `.zip` you downloaded from an open-data portal is usually already in the right shape and can be dropped in as it is.

list: Feature classes, including those inside feature datasets, are listed as layers.
Standalone tables are listed and export as CSV.
Domains and subtypes are not applied: you get the stored codes, not the descriptions.
Topologies, network datasets, relationship classes and raster datasets are skipped.
Personal geodatabases (`.mdb`) and enterprise geodatabase connections (`.sde`) are different formats and are not supported.

body.h2: Shapefile limits to keep in mind
p: Geodatabase field names can be 64 characters; Shapefile allows 10, so long names are shortened. Shapefiles also top out at 2 GB per file and drop the time part of date fields. For anything large or with long field names, GeoPackage is the better target.

title: GDB to GeoJSON Converter Online: File Geodatabase to GeoJSON | GeoUnpack
description: Convert Esri file geodatabase feature classes to GeoJSON (WGS84) online. Free, runs in your browser, nothing uploaded.
lead: Export feature classes from a zipped .gdb to GeoJSON for web maps, Python or JavaScript.
steps: Compress the .gdb folder to a .zip.
Drop the .zip into the box.
Select layers, choose 'GeoJSON' and click Convert & download.
faq: Can I convert several feature classes at once?
Yes. Select several layers and they are exported into one .zip, one GeoJSON file per layer.
subtitle: Convert file geodatabase feature classes to GeoJSON (WGS84).

p: Each feature class becomes one GeoJSON `FeatureCollection` in WGS84 longitude/latitude with six-decimal precision, as RFC 7946 requires. Field names are kept in full. If you tick several feature classes they are delivered together in one `.zip`, one `.geojson` per feature class.

The files load directly with `L.geoJSON()` in Leaflet, as a `geojson` source in Mapbox GL or MapLibre, and with `geopandas.read_file()` in Python. Geodatabase date fields are written as ISO 8601 strings, and coded-value domains come through as their stored codes. For feature classes with hundreds of thousands of features, GeoJSON gets large and slow; GeoPackage is the better exchange format in that case, and geopandas reads it the same way.

Excel shows at most 1,048,576 rows. Larger tables are complete in the file but Excel will not display them all.
Excel may turn long ID numbers into scientific notation or drop leading zeros; import those columns as Text.

faq: When should I use a cloud converter instead?
For very large files, raster data or formats GeoUnpack doesn't support yet. For sensitive data or quick Esri package conversions, local conversion is simpler and safer.
subtitle: An alternative to cloud GIS converters for Esri packages: nothing is uploaded.

p: Many Esri packages people need to convert are not theirs to share: parcel data from a client, utility networks, unpublished survey results, data under a licence or a non-disclosure agreement. Uploading such a file to any third-party server can breach those terms, however trustworthy the service is. GeoUnpack avoids the question, because the file is read by code running in your own browser tab and is never sent anywhere. You can confirm this in your browser's developer tools: the Network tab shows no upload.

GeoUnpack does one job: getting vector data out of `.lpk`, `.lpkx`, `.mpk`, `.mpkx` and zipped `.gdb` files. General cloud converters cover far more formats, handle rasters, offer coordinate-system options and can process files larger than a browser's memory allows. If you need those, a cloud converter or desktop QGIS is the right tool.

faq: What is the difference between KML and KMZ?
A KMZ is a zip file containing a KML named doc.kml. The content is identical; the KMZ is several times smaller, which matters for e-mail attachments and for Google My Maps' 5 MB import limit.
Are symbology and labels kept?
No. GeoUnpack exports the geometry and attributes. Colours and labels from ArcGIS are not carried over; Google Earth applies its default style.

p: KML is verbose XML text, so a detailed polygon layer quickly reaches tens of megabytes. Compressed as KMZ, the same data is typically 5 to 10 times smaller. Google Earth Pro, Google Earth on the web and Google My Maps all open KMZ directly, and it is the format most people mean when they ask for a 'Google Earth file'.

title: MPKX Viewer: Open .mpkx Files Online Without ArcGIS Pro | GeoUnpack
description: Open an ArcGIS Pro .mpkx map package in your browser without ArcGIS Pro. List every layer and table, preview it on a map, export to Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or CSV.
subtitle: Open ArcGIS Pro map packages (.mpkx), browse every layer and export the data. No ArcGIS Pro needed.
lead: An .mpkx file is a map package created by ArcGIS Pro. It bundles a map and a copy of every layer's data. Drop it below to see the layers inside and export them to formats any GIS can read.
steps: Drop the .mpkx file into the box.
Click Preview on any layer to see it on the map.
Tick the layers you need, pick a format and click Convert & download.
faq: What is an .mpkx file?
A map package from ArcGIS Pro: a 7-Zip archive containing the map definition (.mapx) and the data of every layer, usually in file geodatabases. It replaced ArcMap's .mpk format.
How do I open an .mpkx file in ArcGIS Pro?
Double-click it, or drag it into a Pro project; Pro unpacks it into your Documents\ArcGIS\Packages folder. Without ArcGIS Pro, use this viewer to get the data out.
Can I open an .mpkx in ArcMap or QGIS?
Neither opens it directly. ArcMap cannot read Pro packages at all. For QGIS, export the layers to GeoPackage here, or unpack the .mpkx with 7-Zip and load the .gdb folder inside.

p: Unpacked, an `.mpkx` holds a `.mapx` file (the map, in JSON), an `esriinfo` folder with metadata, and the data in folders named after the ArcGIS Pro version, such as `p20` or `p30`, plus `commondata`. The data is almost always one or more file geodatabases. GeoUnpack reads them all, keeps only the newest copy when data is duplicated, and lists one row per layer or table.

`.mpk` is the older ArcMap map package; `.mpkx` is the ArcGIS Pro version. ArcGIS Pro opens both, ArcMap only `.mpk`. For getting the data out they behave the same, and GeoUnpack opens either. The map layout, symbology and labels are stored in the `.mapx` and are not converted; you get the geometry and attributes.

Some `.mpkx` files reference data on a server or an enterprise geodatabase instead of containing a copy, and some contain only rasters or web layers. GeoUnpack will tell you when it finds no vector data. Ask the sender to re-create the package with the option to include the data.

faq: What is an .lpkx file?
A layer package created by ArcGIS Pro. It is a 7-Zip archive containing a .lyrx layer definition (symbology, in JSON) and the layer's data, usually as a file geodatabase.
What opens .lpkx files?
ArcGIS Pro opens them directly. ArcMap cannot. QGIS cannot open the package itself, but it can read the file geodatabase inside once the package is unpacked, or a GeoPackage exported here.

p: The archive contains a `.lyrx` file with the layer's styling, an `esriinfo` folder with metadata and a thumbnail, and the data in version folders such as `p20` or `p30`. GeoUnpack unpacks it in your browser, reads the geodatabase with GDAL and shows each layer's geometry type, feature count and coordinate system.

Export to Shapefile for older software, KML or KMZ for Google Earth, GeoJSON for web maps, or CSV for Excel.
Elevation, imagery and other raster layers inside an .lpkx are not supported yet.
